findings.explanation: The hook presents the quotation as a claim made about the law as it stands. The package's own transcript window around this quote has the speaker introducing "what heat pump tax credits are available in 2024" under "the bill that was signed" (the Inflation Reduction Act), and hedging the sentence with "technically"; the IRS passage the Short cites says the termination of 25C was accelerated. The Short drops both the parent's "In an earlier video" (s23) and the speaker's "technically", so a viewer who sees only this Short hears a channel asserting today that the credit runs to 2033 and concludes the channel was wrong about the law. What the passages establish is different: the statement was true of the law as it then stood and a 2025 law cut the credit short. Nothing later in a Short corrects this, and the title repeats it in the present tense ("runs through 2033").
findings.suggestion: Date the quotation and keep its hedge, as the parent's s23 does: 'In an earlier video, The Thought Provocateur told viewers "technically these heat pump tax credits based on the bill that was signed are available through 2033".' Reword the script title the same way ("An earlier video said the heat pump tax credit ran through 2033. The IRS says it ended in 2025."). With the s03 fix below this costs about 14 words across the Short, taking it to roughly 55 seconds at 150 wpm: inside the 60-second cap, so trim wording rather than adding anything new.

findings.explanation: The cited passage says OBBB "accelerated the termination" of the 25C credit, and the package's NPR statement says the credits "were supposed to last until the 2030s" before the 2025 law "sunseted the credits much earlier on December 31st, 2025". The assertion s03.a carries "whose termination was accelerated", but the narration reports only the end date; the parent's s25 says "But it was cut short" and the Short drops it. Paired with the hook, a viewer comes away believing the credit was never available past 2025 and that the quoted channel invented 2033 - the opposite of what the IRS passage establishes. In a Short no later sentence supplies it.
findings.suggestion: Restore the parent's clause: "But it was cut short: the IRS says the credit is not allowed for any property placed in service after December 31, 2025 ..." - four words, already entailed by the cited passage and by the assertion's own wording.

findings.explanation: The cited passage reads "The credit is allowed for qualifying property placed in service on or after Jan. 1, 2023, and before December 31, 2025", and the same IRS page adds (lines 27-31) that for 2025 no credit is allowed for an item unless it was produced by a qualified manufacturer and the taxpayer reports its QMID. The narration drops "qualifying" and states entitlement outright ("keeps the credit"), so it tells every owner of a pre-deadline heat pump they have the credit, which the passage establishes only for qualifying property. The parent's s25 avoided this by stating the negative case ("a heat pump installed after that date cannot claim it").
findings.suggestion: Say "a qualifying heat pump in service before that deadline can still claim it".

findings.explanation: The percentage is spoken with no denominator: "30 percent of a qualifying heat pump". The passage says the credit "equals 30% of certain qualified expenses" with a $2,000 annual cap for qualified heat pumps, the package's carry for this Short words it "30 percent of the cost of a qualifying heat pump", and the parent's s24 says "30 percent of the cost of". The carry is otherwise made in the Short, so this is imprecision rather than a missing carry, but as spoken the figure has no measure.
findings.suggestion: Say "30 percent of the cost of a qualifying heat pump, capped at $2,000 a year from 2023".

findings.explanation: The sentence is accurate about the cited passage - the termination table lists code sections 25C and 25D and no rebate programme - and it does carry the Short's third qualification. But "with no state or utility rebate on the list" is an argument from absence, and in a Short the inference a viewer draws is that rebates are the surviving route. The parent answers that over s26 to s30; this Short cannot. The package's own DOE Program Notice 26-2 removes the federal electric-home rebate allowance for fuel-switching (rebates now only for upgrading from existing electric equipment), so the inference is wrong for exactly the viewer replacing a gas furnace.
findings.suggestion: Make the same carry without the implicature and at the same length: "And what ended is federal: the IRS lists it by code section, 25C beside 25D; state and utility rebates are separate programmes with their own rules." Do not add that any rebate is still open - the package holds no verdict on one, and its gaps say so.
